pharm: A red, non-provitamin-A carotenoid pigment found in tomatoes, watermelon, and other red fruits, valued as a lipid-soluble antioxidant. It is used as a dietary supplement (often as an antioxidant and for prostate/cardiovascular health claims) and is not an FDA-approved drug.

Generally none for dietary use; assess need/expectations of supplementation
summary: Lycopene is a fat-soluble carotenoid pigment that gives tomatoes and other fruits their red color. It is a potent antioxidant that quenches reactive oxygen species (notably singlet oxygen) and is taken as a dietary supplement for general antioxidant support and for popularly claimed benefits in prostate health, cardiovascular health, and skin protection, although clinical evidence is mixed. Unlike beta-carotene it has no provitamin A activity. It is regulated as a dietary supplement, not an FDA-approved medicine, so there is no officially established therapeutic dose; typical supplement intakes are in the range of a few to tens of milligrams per day. Absorption is improved by dietary fat and by cooking/processing (e.g., tomato paste). It is generally regarded as safe; very high intakes can cause harmless orange skin discoloration (lycopenemia).
indications: Popular supplement use for prostate and cardiovascular health and skin photoprotection (evidence mixed; not an FDA-approved drug indication)

moa: Lycopene is an acyclic carotenoid with 11 conjugated double bonds, making it one of the most efficient biological quenchers of singlet oxygen and a scavenger of free radicals. By neutralizing reactive oxygen species it may reduce oxidative damage to lipids, proteins, and DNA. Proposed additional actions include modulation of cell-signaling and gap-junction communication, anti-inflammatory effects, and influences on lipid metabolism. It does not have provitamin A activity. These mechanisms underlie its proposed but not definitively proven health benefits.

relative: Caution with high-dose supplements in pregnancy/lactation (limited safety data)
Theoretical caution with very high doses before surgery (possible mild antiplatelet/blood-pressure effects)
monitor: Generally none required for dietary/supplemental use

preg: Lycopene consumed in normal dietary amounts (from foods) is considered safe in pregnancy. There is insufficient safety information for high-dose lycopene supplements, so concentrated supplements should be avoided or used only under professional advice during pregnancy.
lact: Lycopene in normal dietary amounts is considered safe during breastfeeding and is naturally present in breast milk. There is limited information on high-dose supplements; use concentrated supplements cautiously and preferably under professional advice.
renal: No dose adjustment is required in renal impairment for dietary or usual supplemental intake.
hepatic: No dose adjustment is required in hepatic impairment for dietary or usual supplemental intake.

minor: Beta-carotene - may compete with lycopene for absorption when taken together in large amounts
Cholesterol-lowering agents (e.g., cholestyramine, plant sterols, orlistat) - may reduce absorption of fat-soluble carotenoids
Antihypertensive or antiplatelet drugs - theoretical additive effect at high doses (clinically minor)
interactions.food: Absorption is increased by dietary fat and by cooking/processing; taking with a fatty meal improves uptake.
interactions.diagnostics: Very high intake can cause an orange skin discoloration (lycopenemia) that may be mistaken for jaundice but spares the sclerae.

common: Occasional mild GI upset at high doses
rare: Lycopenemia/lycopenodermia - reversible orange skin discoloration with very high intake

monitoring: No specific monitoring required for dietary or usual supplemental use
counsel: Lycopene is an antioxidant found in tomatoes and other red fruits, taken as a supplement for general health
Take it with a meal that has some fat so your body absorbs it better
Cooked tomato products like sauce and paste are rich, well-absorbed sources
It is generally very safe; very large amounts can turn the skin a harmless orange color that fades when you cut back
It is a dietary supplement, not a proven medicine - tell your doctor if you are using it for a specific health condition
If pregnant or breastfeeding, get dietary lycopene from food and check with your clinician before high-dose supplements

pearls: Lycopene is a non-provitamin-A carotenoid and one of the most efficient singlet-oxygen quenchers among dietary antioxidants
Bioavailability is higher from cooked/processed tomato products and when taken with fat
Regulated as a dietary supplement, NOT an FDA-approved drug; no officially established therapeutic dose
Evidence for prostate and cardiovascular benefit is mixed and not conclusive
Very high intake causes harmless reversible orange skin (lycopenodermia) without scleral involvement (unlike jaundice)
missed: If you miss a dose, take it when you remember or simply continue the next day. Do not take a double dose. Missing a dose of a dietary supplement is not harmful.
overdose: Lycopene has very low toxicity. Excessive intake may cause mild gastrointestinal upset and a harmless reversible orange discoloration of the skin (lycopenodermia), which resolves on reducing intake. No specific treatment is needed beyond stopping or reducing the supplement.
